manufacturer_data.description: Yale (0x01D1) or ASSA ABLOY (0x012E). Locks advertise the 0xFE24 service.

device.name: Yale Access / August Smart Locks
device.notes:
August / Yale Access smart locks (August Smart Lock, Pro, Wi-Fi Smart Lock, Yale Assure with a Yale Access module). There is no official local API — the vendor posture is closed — but direct BLE lock/unlock works once a client holds the lock's OFFLINE KEY and key slot (index). Those must be pulled from an August/Yale account (a cloud login), after which day-to-day unlock is fully local. yalexs-ble is the reference local implementation (Home Assistant's "Yale Access Bluetooth").
GATT: primary service 0000fe24-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb; write bd4ac611-0b45-11e3-8ffd-0800200c9a66, read bd4ac612-..., secure-write bd4ac613-..., secure-read bd4ac614-.... Yale company id 0x01D1 (465).
FRAMING: every GATT command and response is 18 bytes. Normal-session operation requests begin 0xEE, carry the opcode at byte[1], and use a one-byte additive checksum at byte[3] chosen so all 18 bytes sum to zero mod 256. Command opcodes: 0x02 GETSTATUS, 0x03 WRITESETTING, 0x04 READSETTING, 0x0A UNLOCK, 0x0B LOCK, 0x2D GETLOG. GETLOG pops the oldest activity record; it is not a passive read. The advertisement's HAP-derived 0x06/0x11 markers are not the normal GATT operation-frame leader.
CRYPTO/AUTH: the secure-channel handshake first uses the offline key and keyIndex (slot), exchanges two 8-byte random halves, and combines them into a 16-byte session key. The two handshake exchanges use AES-ECB. Later normal-session operation payloads use that session key with independent, persistent client-to-lock and lock-to-client CBC chains. Each chain starts with a 16-byte all-zero IV only when the key is installed, continues across consecutive frames, and resets on reconnect. If the key or slot is wrong the lock rejects the exchange. Motor result is read at response byte[15] (0x00 success; 0x1E-0x23 jam/mechanical failure).

openness.notes: No published local protocol; local control depends on an offline key the vendor cloud holds. The BLE stack was reverse-engineered and is mature (in production in Home Assistant). The CBC design, which starts each session with a zero IV and then chains frames, has drawn security scrutiny historically; no fresh advisory URL was verified for this spec, so none is asserted here.

enter_pairing_mode.notes: There is no pairing-mode button in this flow. Authorisation is issued by the vendor account rather than by possession of the lock, which is the opposite of the Nuki model and worth knowing before someone goes looking for a button to hold.

exclusivity.recovery: Close the Yale Access app before connecting; it holds the lock while it is in the foreground. Do not drive the same lock from HomeKit and from a yalexs-ble client on one host: Home Assistant's docs say the two contend for the lock and both fail.

pairing.notes: The gate is an offline key and slot number, not a Bluetooth bond. The lock runs a secure handshake keyed by that offline key; a client gets the key either from the August/Yale cloud with an account that has owner-level access (what the Home Assistant integrations do) or by extracting it from a phone where the vendor app has stored it. Once held, lock and unlock are entirely local, which is what makes this lock survivable if the vendor service is not — with the caveat that the key can rotate underneath a client, and only the account can issue the new one. Medium confidence: Home Assistant's Yale Access Bluetooth integration and yalexs-ble implement this in production; this project has not driven a lock.

pin.notes: The lock's OFFLINE KEY and key slot index, synchronised to a client that has logged into an August/Yale account. Per-unit key material, so no value appears here. Once held, unlocking is fully local and the account is not consulted again — which is what makes this lock survivable if the vendor service does not.

unpair.clears: Access through the revoked or rotated key; the lock's settings stay.
unpair.notes: Revocation is account-side, and it happens to local clients whether or not anyone intends it. Owners remove users and devices in the vendor app (how and when that reaches the lock's key slots is not documented in the sources used here), and the keys themselves rotate: Home Assistant's documentation warns that a phone that operates the lock often can rotate the key, after which a client holding the old offline key fails the handshake until it re-syncs from the account. Treat an authentication failure as a stale key, not a fault. A factory reset clears every slot (see `setup.factory_reset`).

issued_to_client: The offline key + slot (synced from the August/Yale cloud account)
credentials.notes: The offline key is the crown jewel: it starts the AES-ECB setup that derives the session key used by later AES-CBC operations, and it is held by the vendor cloud, so obtaining it requires an account. The Wi-Fi variants add a separate radio/bridge; the lock core here is BLE.
stored_on_device: Offline key material + key slots (enrolled devices)

factory_reset.description:
Read the procedure for the specific model before starting: all three families below need the batteries out, and two of them need the interior escutcheon off the door to reach a button that is not externally accessible. That is deliberate on the vendor's part — a reset that could be done from outside would be a way past the lock — and it means this is not something to attempt on a door someone needs to use in the next ten minutes.
A lock previously enrolled in a Z-Wave network should be excluded from that network as well; a reset clears the lock's side but not the controller's.
factory_reset.effect: Deletes every user code including the Master code, clears enrolled clients and their offline keys, and returns all programming to factory defaults. On the Assure models, creating a new Master code is the only thing the lock will accept afterwards and must be done before anything else.

procedures.basis: Yale's installation guide for the Assure Lock 2 key-free deadbolt.
procedures.name: Assure Lock 2 Key Free Deadbolt: reset tool held for one minute

steps.action: Remove the battery cover and take out one battery.
Press the reset button for one full minute with the reset tool supplied in the hardware box.
Replace the battery and the cover.

procedures.basis: Yale's installation guide for the Assure Lock for Andersen doors.
procedures.name: Assure Lock (Andersen): reset button held across a battery insertion

steps.action: Remove the battery cover and all batteries.
Remove the interior lock body to reach the reset button, which sits above the PCB cable connectors.
Re-insert three batteries and hold the reset button for three seconds.
Still holding, insert the fourth battery and hold for a further three seconds, then release.
Re-install the interior lock on the door.
steps.expect: The lock accepts only Master PIN code creation until a new Master code is set.

procedures.name: Assure Lock SL: reset button held while the batteries go back in

steps.action: Remove the battery cover and all batteries.
Remove the interior side of the lock to reach the reset button, which sits beside the cable adapter.
Press and hold the reset button for at least three seconds while reinstalling the batteries, then release.

steps.expect: The lock accepts only Master Entry code creation until a new Master code is set.

cloud.local_alternative: Yes for control — once the offline key + slot are synced from the cloud, lock/unlock is entirely local over BLE. The offline key itself can only be obtained from an August/Yale account; there is no documented account-free way to get it.

methods.description: Obtain the lock's offline key + slot from an August/Yale account (a one-time cloud step), then run the BLE secure handshake (0x01/0x03) and send LOCK (0x0B) / UNLOCK (0x0A) as AES-CBC-encrypted frames.

steps.action: Enroll the lock in the August/Yale app and sync the account so it holds the offline keys.
Extract the offline key + key slot via the account (e.g. the yalexs integration).
Run the BLE secure handshake, then send UNLOCK (0x0A) / LOCK (0x0B) as AES-CBC frames.

setup.notes: Enroll the lock in the August/Yale app, then log the account into a client that can sync the OFFLINE KEY + key slot from the cloud (this is what Home Assistant's august/yalexs integration does; a fresh owner account may be needed to force the keys to synchronize). Hand those to a local BLE client for offline unlock thereafter.

rejoin.notes: No network membership on the lock; a client with the offline key re-connects independently.

testing.notes: Not driven against hardware by this project. The GATT UUIDs, HAP-derived framing, opcodes and stateful AES-CBC session crypto are from Yale-Libs/yalexs-ble; the offline-key requirement from the Home Assistant integration docs.

consumer_limitations.reason: The schema's characteristic value/template model and the generic mobile client have no transform for a session key, persistent independent CBC chains, or reconnect reset. Exposing the application frames below as raw commands would write plaintext and fail or desynchronise the session. They are documentation for a session-aware implementation, not generic executable commands. Do not add entity bindings until that transform and its state lifecycle are supported by the consumer.

application_frame.note: These are application-layer plaintext inputs to the session wrapper, not on-wire GATT values. Compute the simple checksum with byte 3 zero.

get_door_and_lock_status.description: Read combined door and lock state (opcode 0x02, subtype 0x2F).

get_unread_activity_count.description: Read unread activity count (opcode 0x02, subtype 0x09). Unlike GETLOG (0x2D), this does not consume activity records.

normal_operation.chaining: Persist each direction's CBC state across every consecutive command or response on that connection. The previous ciphertext block is the next block's chaining input. Two consecutive frames therefore do not use independent zero-IV encryptions.
normal_operation.key: 16-byte session key derived by the secure handshake
normal_operation.key_installation: On session-key installation, create independent client-to-lock and lock-to-client CBC contexts. Each direction starts with a 16-byte all-zero IV exactly once. Do not reset the IV for each command or response, and do not share one context between directions.
normal_operation.reconnect: A reconnect tears down both contexts. Re-run session-key installation and restart both chains from zero IV; never carry CBC state across connections. A partial or poisoned block likewise requires a reconnect and fresh context, not a zero-IV rewrite of just the next frame.

checksum.formula: (-(LE32(frame[0:4]) + LE32(frame[4:8]) + LE(frame[8:18]))) mod 2^32. The first two terms are 32-bit little-endian words; the third is the entire 80-bit little-endian integer from bytes 8-17. Zero bytes 12-15 before computing, then write the resulting uint32 LE at bytes 12-15. This is not a negated sum of the frame's bytes.

known_answer.origin: Synthetic known-answer vector computed with the reference formula, not a capture.

secure_handshake.initial_key: offline key plus keyIndex (slot), then the derived session key
secure_handshake.trailer: 0F at byte 16 and keyIndex at byte 17

client_to_device.name: lock, first frame after key installation
unlock, second frame on the same TX chain

synthetic_cbc_vectors.description: Deterministic on-wire examples derived with OpenSSL AES-128-CBC and the invented session key 00 01 02 ... 0F. They are full 18-byte GATT values, including each frame's clear two-byte trailer, and demonstrate two consecutive frames on independent TX and RX chains. They are not captures or real key data.

device_to_client.ciphertext_hex: 92 BC 6D 65 B8 40 4B C3 35 DE BA 2C 97 D0 4D BC 02 00
device_to_client.name: read acknowledgement, first frame on the independent RX chain
read answer, second frame on the same RX chain

characteristics.name: Normal operation write
characteristics.notes: Stateful AES-CBC ciphertext only. Do not write the application-layer plaintext frames from protocol_details directly: bytes 0-15 must be encrypted on the continuing client-to-lock chain, while bytes 16-17 remain clear. A fresh zero IV is used only when the session key is installed, not independently for each command.

characteristics.name: Normal operation response
characteristics.notes: Normal-session responses and unsolicited state on an independent, persistent lock-to-client CBC chain. Motor result is byte[15] of a decrypted 0xBB lock/unlock op-response.

characteristics.name: Secure handshake write
characteristics.notes: Setup and shutdown only, not lock/status operations. AES-ECB. Setup starts with the offline key and keyIndex, then switches to the derived 16-byte session key. The exact 32-bit checksum is in protocol_details.session_crypto.secure_handshake; it is not a bytewise checksum.

characteristics.name: Secure handshake response
characteristics.notes: AES-ECB setup and shutdown responses; not the normal motor-result channel.

services.name: August / Yale lock service (0xFE24)
services.notes: Two channels share this service. The normal operation channel (bd4ac611/bd4ac612) carries 18-byte command and response frames after the handshake, encrypted with AES-CBC under the derived session key. The secure channel (bd4ac613/bd4ac614) is for setup and shutdown, initially encrypted with AES-ECB under the offline key and then under the derived session key. Operation results arrive at response byte[15]. The generic command/entity model has no stateful CBC transform, so this service deliberately exposes no executable characteristic commands or entities.
